docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Switches every process sees at once: circuit breakers, maintenance mode and feature flags.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Circuit breakers
docs.text:
FastAPIBreaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing (a database, an SDK, a service reached without httpx), so that requests fail at once instead of waiting for it, and it gets room to recover:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIBreaker

payments = FastAPIBreaker("payments", failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=30, timeout=10)


@payments
async def charge(order: Order) -> Receipt:
    return await payments_sdk.charge(order.id, order.total)


async def refund(order: Order) -> None:
    async with payments.attempt():  # or around a block
        await payments_sdk.refund(order.id)
  • States: after failure_threshold consecutive failures it opens, and for reset_timeout seconds calls fail with BreakerOpen without reaching the dependency. Then a single trial call goes through: its success closes the breaker, its failure opens it again.
  • In FastAPI: BreakerOpen is an HTTPException: an endpoint that hits an open breaker answers 503 with Retry-After (the seconds until the trial), without naming the dependency.
  • What counts: exceptions in failures (any Exception by default) are failures; those in exclude mean the dependency answered (a "not found" from its SDK) and are successes; others, and a cancelled call, give no verdict. timeout bounds async calls: a slower call is cancelled, raises TimeoutError and counts as a failure. Sync code can't be interrupted, so a breaker with a timeout refuses to guard it.
  • Per process: each process keeps its own state, with no round trip on every call. Sync functions work too, also from the threads of FastAPI's pool.
  • Closed by hand: payments.reset() closes it at once and forgets the failures, when you know the dependency is back (from an admin endpoint) or between tests; failure_threshold and reset_timeout can be read back.
  • Observability: opening is logged as a warning and closing again as info, and both are counted with the calls (fastapi_alcazaba.breaker.* metrics). breaker.state says "closed", "open" or "half-open", handy in a health check: HealthCheck(lambda: payments.state != "open", critical=False).

docs.title: Maintenance mode
docs.text:
FastAPIMaintenance is a switch shared by every process; while it's on, MaintenanceMiddleware answers 503 with Retry-After to every request but the allowed ones:

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import client_ip
from fastapi_alcazaba.operations import FastAPIMaintenance, MaintenanceMiddleware

maintenance = FastAPIMaintenance()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIMaintenance(cache)
app.add_middleware(
    MaintenanceMiddleware,
    maintenance=maintenance,
    allow_paths=("/health", "/admin"),  # always served
    allow=lambda request: client_ip(request) in OFFICE,  # the team keeps working
)

await maintenance.enable("Back at 10:30", retry_after=900)  # from an admin route, a script...
await (
    maintenance.status()
)  # MaintenanceStatus(enabled=True, message=..., retry_after=900, since=...)
await maintenance.disable()
  • Shared, but not asked on every request: the state lives in the backend, and each process keeps a copy refreshed at most every refresh seconds (1 by default), so a change reaches every process within about that. status() reads the backend now; forget() drops the copy, and a new cache drops it by itself (each test's lifespan sets one up).
  • Responses: a 503 whose detail is the message ("Service Unavailable" without one), with Retry-After when given and Cache-Control: no-store. WebSockets are closed with 1013 (try again later). Lifespan events go through. A pure ASGI middleware: streaming isn't affected.
  • Exceptions: allow_paths are prefixes (/health covers /health/live, not /healthz), matched without the root_path of a proxy or a mount, and are served without reading the state. allow (sync or async) receives the request: use the address the server reports (client_ip), never X-Forwarded-For.
  • Failures: when the backend fails, each process keeps the last state it read (maintenance often means work on the backend itself: its failure mustn't reopen an app closed on purpose) and serves normally if it never read one. enable() and disable() raise BackendUnavailable: nothing changes then.
  • Integrity: with a signing_key or encryption_key on the cache the state is sealed, and a state planted in the backend by someone else is ignored; the message is capped at 1000 characters.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.text:
FastAPIFeatureFlags keeps flags in the backend: turn features on and off for everybody, for some users or tenants, or for a percentage of them, from any process and without a deploy:

from fastapi_alcazaba.operations import FastAPIFeatureFlags

flags = FastAPIFeatureFlags()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIFeatureFlags(cache, refresh=5)

await flags.set("new-checkout", enabled=True, percentage=10, allow=["user-42"], deny=["user-7"])

if await flags.enabled("new-checkout", subject=str(user.id)):
    ...


def user_id(request: Request) -> str | None:
    return request.headers.get("x-user-id")


@app.get("/beta/report", dependencies=[Depends(flags.require("beta-report", subject=user_id))])
async def beta_report() -> Report: ...  # 404 while the flag is off for the user
  • Rules: a flag is on for a subject when it's enabled, the subject isn't in deny, and it's in allow or falls within percentage. No percentage means everybody, but only allow when there's an allow list: a flag for a few never goes to everyone by mistake. enabled=False turns it off for everyone, allow included. Without a subject, a partial rollout counts as off. An undefined flag gives default (False).
  • Sticky rollouts: a subject's place comes from a hash of the flag's name and the subject, so it keeps its answer while the percentage stays, raising the percentage only adds subjects, and each flag picks different subjects.
  • Hidden when off: require() answers FastAPI's own 404 Not Found, so the flag isn't revealed, and closes WebSockets with 1008. For subjects that need other dependencies (the current user), call enabled() from your own dependency.
  • Local copies: each process keeps the definitions it reads for refresh seconds (5), so a change reaches every process within that, and a flag costs at most one round trip per refresh. When the backend fails, the last definition read is used, or the default. get(name) reads the backend now; delete(name) removes a flag; forget() drops the copies, and a new cache drops them by itself.
  • Privacy and integrity: subjects are stored as SHA-256 digests salted with the flag's name, never in clear (at most 10,000 per list). Whoever reads the backend can still confirm a guess of a guessable subject (an e-mail address): prefer opaque ids, or give the cache an encryption_key, which encrypts the definitions. With a signing_key or encryption_key, definitions planted by someone else are ignored. Names are up to 100 letters, digits, ., _ and -.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

Three tools, with nothing but FastAPI and pydantic: FastAPIPagination (?page=2&size=20), FastAPIPaginationLimitOffset (?limit=20&offset=40) and FastAPIPaginationCursor (?size=20&cursor=...). Each is configured once and used as a dependency, which reads and checks the query parameters; the endpoint gets them as an argument, so @cache keeps each page under a key of its own:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIPagination
from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination import Page, PageParams

pages = FastAPIPagination(default_size=20, max_size=100)


@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["products"])
async def products(params: Annotated[PageParams, Depends(pages)]) -> Page[Product]:
    return pages.paginate(await load_products(), params)

GET /products?page=2&size=20 answers {"items": [...], "total": 245, "page": 2, "size": 20, "pages": 13}.

  • Links: the response links to the first, previous, next and last pages in the Link header (RFC 8288), as GitHub's API does: </products?page=3&size=20>; rel="next". The links keep the request's other query parameters and leave out the host, so they don't depend on the Host header nor on a proxy in front. Pages served from the cache get them too, made for the request they answer.
  • From a database: query only the page and give the total: pages.paginate(rows, params, total=count), with params.offset and params.limit in the query. Without total, paginate slices the page from the whole list.
  • Limit and offset: FastAPIPaginationLimitOffset(default_limit=..., max_limit=...) gives LimitOffsetParams and makes LimitOffsetPages, the same way.
  • Limits: each tool has its own (max_size, max_limit; 100 by default), so that nobody asks for a million rows at once: anything beyond, or malformed, is a 422 before the endpoint runs. They're in the OpenAPI schema too.
  • Coming from fastapi-pagination: the JSON is that of its Page and LimitOffsetPage, so clients don't change. Its add_pagination keeps the page parameters out of the endpoint's arguments, in a context variable: a cache that only sees the arguments can't tell the pages apart, and would serve page 1 for every page.

docs.title: By cursor
docs.text:
A cursor points at the last item of a page by its sort key, not by its position: rows added or deleted meanwhile don't shift the pages (no item skipped or seen twice), and a database finds any page through an index, as fast as the first. For infinite scroll, feeds and clients that sync everything:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIPaginationCursor
from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination import CursorPage, CursorParams

cursors = FastAPIPaginationCursor(secret=settings.cursor_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.get("/events")
@cache(expire=60)
async def events(params: Annotated[CursorParams, Depends(cursors)]) -> CursorPage[Event]:
    query = select(Event).order_by(Event.created_at, Event.id).limit(params.limit)
    if params.after is not None:  # (created_at, id) of the last event seen
        query = query.where(tuple_(Event.created_at, Event.id) > params.after)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return cursors.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda e: (e.created_at, e.id), queried=True)

GET /events?size=20 answers {"items": [...], "size": 20, "next_cursor": "WyIyMDI2..."}, and ?cursor=<next_cursor> the next page; next_cursor is null on the last one. The Link header has the first page and, except on the last page, the next one.

  • The sort key (key) must be unique: (created_at, id), not created_at alone, which two items may share. Its values can be strings, integers (up to 64 bits), floats, booleans, datetimes, dates, UUIDs and decimals, and params.after has them back as such.
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those of the page, queried with a key past params.after and params.limit (one more than size: it tells whether there's a next page). Without it, paginate finds the page in the whole sorted list. descending=True for newest first.
  • Signed: with a secret, cursors carry an HMAC-SHA256 and a client can't make one up or change it; a list rotates secrets. Without it, a cursor's values are checked to be of those types. Either way an invalid cursor is a 400, and one longer than 1024 characters or malformed a 422, before the endpoint runs. Cursors are base64, not encrypted: clients can read the sort key, so sort by what they may see.
  • Forward only: to go back, clients keep the cursors they've used.

Every page, size and filter is one entry: tag them (tags=["products"]) to drop them all when the data changes. For short lists, caching the whole list with get_or_set and slicing every page from it keeps a single entry. The pagination example does all three, with the database session left out of the key (exclude_params).

docs.title: Security model and resilience
docs.text:
What the cache stores and for whom, what it trusts the backend with, and what happens when the backend fails.

Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
• What gets cached: GET requests (any call for plain functions) whose response is a 200 and doesn't say Cache-Control: no-store.
  • Per-user data: requests are told apart by the endpoint's arguments plus the vary_headers. If a response depends on anything else (request.state, a header that isn't in vary_headers, the client IP…), add it to vary_headers or to a custom key builder.
  • The backend is trusted for availability, not for integrity: without a signing_key or an encryption_key, whoever can write to it decides what your endpoints return. Use one whenever the backend is shared or reachable by others, and always with PickleCoder.
  • Confidentiality: signed entries are readable by whoever can read the backend, its dumps (RDB/AOF files) and backups. When responses carry personal or sensitive data, use encryption_key instead.
  • Keys built by the default key builder are SHA-256 digests: arguments and tokens never appear in the backend in clear text.
  • Fail open: if the backend is down or an entry can't be decoded, the endpoint runs as if there were no cache. Rate limiters let requests through too, unless fail_open=False.
  • Rate limits count clients by the address the ASGI server gives, IPv6 by /64 (configure it to trust your proxy, and only it), or by your identifier. Whoever can write to the backend can reset them; clear() can't.

Report vulnerabilities as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Resilience
docs.text:
The cache never makes a request fail. Every backend call has a timeout (backend_timeout, 1 s by default): if it runs out, or the backend fails, the request goes on without cache. After circuit_breaker_failures consecutive failures the backend isn't called at all for circuit_breaker_reset seconds, so that requests don't each wait for the timeout; then one call tries again.

Concurrent misses for the same key compute once per process (single_flight). With several processes or containers, distributed_lock=True makes the first one take a lock in Redis/Valkey while the others wait for its value (up to lock_wait seconds). And early_refresh=0.1 lets callers refresh an entry, with growing probability, during the last 10 % of its lifetime: popular entries are renewed before they expire, instead of every caller missing at once. If that refresh fails, the cached value is served.

docs.title: Checking uploads
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

The name and the Content-Type of an upload are whatever the client chose: an HTML page sent as cat.png would be served back as HTML. FastAPIUploads checks the file itself, with nothing but the standard library:

from fastapi_alcazaba.uploads import IMAGES, CheckedFile, FastAPIUploads

uploads = FastAPIUploads(types=IMAGES, max_size=5 * 1024 * 1024, max_pixels=25_000_000)


@app.post("/avatars")
async def avatar(upload: Annotated[CheckedFile, Depends(uploads)]) -> dict[str, str]:
    name = f"{uuid4()}{upload.extension}"  # never the client's name
    await storage.save(name, upload.file.file, content_type=upload.content_type)
    return {"name": name}

As a dependency it reads the form field file; for other fields or several files, call await uploads.check(file). It returns a CheckedFile: the UploadFile read back to its start, the content_type found in its bytes, its size, its width and height (images) and a safe filename.

  • The real type (sniff(data)): PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, PDF, ZIP, GZIP, MP4 and QuickTime from their signatures; Word, Excel and PowerPoint documents from the content types their [Content_Types].xml declares (as Office reads them), with the macro-enabled ones (.docm, .xlsm, .pptm) told apart, and anything ambiguous reported as a plain ZIP; UTF-8 text without control characters (text/plain: CSV is text, it can't be told apart). Text that starts with a tag is HTML, SVG or XML, never plain text, and SVG is never an image: all three can carry scripts. types must come from KNOWN_TYPES (IMAGES, OFFICE_DOCUMENTS...), so a typo like image/jpg fails at start-up. Store and serve files with the detected type, never the client's, plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (SecurityHeadersMiddleware).
  • Size: counted while the file is read in chunks, whatever UploadFile.size says; 413 beyond max_size, 415 for a type that isn't allowed, 422 for an empty file. By the time an endpoint runs the multipart parser has stored the whole request already, so limit it with BodySizeLimitMiddleware on the route as well.
  • Decompression bombs: the width and height of PNG, JPEG (however much metadata comes before the frame), GIF and WebP images are read from their headers (image_size(data)) without decoding them; more than max_pixels (40 million by default) gets a 413, and an image whose dimensions can't be read a 415.
  • Safe names (safe_filename(name)): NFKC-normalised, only the last path component, without control or invisible characters (such as the right-to-left override that shows exe.txt as txt.exe), <>:"|?* replaced, without leading dots or dashes, _ in front of the names Windows reserves (CON, NUL, COM1...), and at most 255 bytes, keeping the extension. For display and Content-Disposition; store files under names of your own (CheckedFile.extension).
  • What it doesn't do: look inside the files. A PDF can carry scripts, Office documents macros, archives may expand to far more than their size, and the frames of a GIF aren't counted. Allow HTML, SVG or XML only to serve them as attachments from another domain.

docs.title: Webhooks and outbound calls
docs.text:
Webhooks signed and verified the Standard Webhooks way, and calls to other services with a deadline, a circuit breaker and SSRF protection.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Signed webhooks
docs.text:
FastAPIWebhooks accepts only webhooks signed with your secret, and each delivery once. WebhookSigner signs the ones you send. Both follow Standard Webhooks, the format of Svix, Supabase, Clerk, Resend, OpenAI and others: webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature: v1,<base64 HMAC-SHA256 of "id.timestamp.body">, with whsec_... secrets.

from fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks import FastAPIWebhooks, WebhookMessage, WebhookSigner

webhooks = FastAPIWebhooks(settings.webhook_secret)  # "whsec_..."


@app.post("/webhooks/payments")
async def payment_event(message: Annotated[WebhookMessage, Depends(webhooks)]) -> None:
    event = message.json()
    ...  # idempotent on message.id: retries of a message keep its id


# Sending them: sign the exact bytes you send.
signer = WebhookSigner(settings.webhook_secret)  # WebhookSigner.generate_secret() makes one
body = json.dumps(event).encode()
await client.post(url, content=body, headers=signer.sign(body))
  • Raw body, still readable: the signature is checked over the body exactly as it arrived, read up to max_body_size bytes (1 MiB; a 413 beyond, and a Content-Length over it is refused before reading). It stays in the request, for message.json() or await request.json(). Validate it with your model there (Event.model_validate_json(message.body)) rather than with a pydantic body parameter: FastAPI reads and validates those before any dependency runs, so the body would be read without the limit, and an unsigned malformed one would get a 422 before its signature is checked. Not a form parameter either, which consumes the body first.
  • Freshness: a timestamp more than tolerance seconds (300) away from the server's clock, in the past or the future, is refused.
  • Constant time, one answer: every signature in the header is compared in constant time against each secret. A wrong signature, a stale timestamp and a replay all get the same 401 ("Invalid webhook"); only missing or malformed headers get a 400.
  • Replays: each accepted delivery (its id and timestamp, as a SHA-256 digest under Cache.state_key) is counted in the cache's backend until its timestamp can't be accepted anymore, so a captured request sent again is refused by every process. Only accepted deliveries are counted: a forged copy can't burn the id of the real one. A retry of the sender has a new timestamp and signature and goes through, as it must after a failed attempt: make the endpoint idempotent on message.id (a unique constraint) if a message must not be processed twice. The backend must support counters, as every built-in backend does.
  • Backend down: a 503 with Retry-After (fail closed): senders retry later, while a replay would run its effects again. fail_open=True accepts correctly signed webhooks without the replay check instead.
  • Rotation: FastAPIWebhooks([new, old]) accepts a signature by either secret; WebhookSigner([new, old]) signs every message with both, so receivers with either secret accept it.
  • Without a dependency: webhooks.verify(headers, body) checks the signature and the timestamp (not replays), for queues and scripts.

docs.title: Outbound calls
docs.text:
ResilientTransport is an httpx transport for the calls your app makes to other services: a deadline for each call and a circuit breaker for each origin. It needs httpx2 (or httpx):

import httpx2 as httpx

from fastapi_alcazaba.outbound import CircuitOpenError, ResilientTransport


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    transport = ResilientTransport(timeout=5, failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=30)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="https://api.example.com") as client:
        app.state.partner_api = client
        yield


@app.get("/quote")
async def quote(request: Request) -> Quote:
    try:
        response = await request.app.state.partner_api.get("/quote")
    except CircuitOpenError:  # the service keeps failing: don't wait for it
        raise HTTPException(503, "Quotes are unavailable, try again later")
    return Quote.model_validate(response.json())
  • Deadline: timeout bounds the whole call, from sending the request to the last byte of the response. httpx's own timeouts are per phase, and its read timeout restarts with every byte, so a server that trickles a byte every few seconds would keep the request open forever. Past the deadline, httpx.TimeoutException. It applies to each request the transport sends: with follow_redirects=True, every hop gets a deadline of its own.
  • Response size: responses are read whole before they're returned, so don't stream large downloads through it. max_response_size caps the bytes read (as received, before decompression); past it, ResponseTooLargeError, an httpx.RequestError.
  • Circuit breaker: each origin (scheme, host and port) has its own. After failure_threshold consecutive failures, calls to that origin fail at once with CircuitOpenError for reset_timeout seconds, without reaching the server; then a single trial call decides whether it's back. CircuitOpenError is an httpx.TransportError, so code that already handles httpx errors handles it too. transport.state(url) says "closed", "open" or "half-open", handy in a health check. failure_threshold=None turns it off.
  • What counts as a failure: the origin's transport errors (connection and protocol errors, timeouts, yours and httpx's) and responses whose status is in failure_statuses (500, 502, 503 and 504 by default), which are still returned to you. Any other response, 4xx included, is a success. Your own errors are neither: an illegal header value (httpx.LocalProtocolError), a URL scheme httpx can't send (httpx.UnsupportedProtocol), an exception from your request body, ResponseTooLargeError. Otherwise anyone who can put a string in an outbound header could switch the integration off for everybody.
  • Your own transport settings: ResilientTransport(httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(verify=..., limits=..., proxy=...)).

docs.title: URLs your users give: SSRF
docs.text:
Calling a URL that a user typed (a webhook endpoint, a link preview, an avatar by URL) lets them make your server call its own network: http://169.254.169.254/ (the cloud's metadata service and its credentials), http://localhost:6379/, an admin panel on 10.0.0.0/8. SSRFGuardTransport only calls the public internet:

from fastapi_alcazaba.outbound import (
    BlockedDestinationError,
    ResilientTransport,
    SSRFGuardTransport,
)

client = httpx.AsyncClient(
    transport=ResilientTransport(SSRFGuardTransport(ports=(443,)), timeout=10),
    follow_redirects=True,
)

try:
    await client.post(subscription.url, content=body, headers=signer.sign(body))
except BlockedDestinationError:
    ...  # tell the user the URL isn't allowed
  • What's refused: a host with any address that isn't public: private, loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16 and its metadata services, fe80::/10), carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10), multicast, reserved, documentation and benchmarking ranges, unique-local IPv6 (fc00::/7, AWS's fd00:ec2::254), and the IPv6 forms of those IPv4 addresses (::ffff:127.0.0.1, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4, Teredo). Literal addresses in URLs are checked without DNS; anything else goes to DNS, so numeric spellings (http://2130706433/, http://0x7f.1/) and localhost are refused for what they resolve to. Also refused: schemes other than http and https and, with ports, other ports. BlockedDestinationError says which host, never the address it resolved to (that's logged instead).
  • Pinned against DNS rebinding: the transport resolves the host itself and connects to the address it checked: the URL is rewritten to it, the Host header keeps the name, and TLS gets the name for SNI and the certificate check. A DNS server that answers a public address to the check and a private one to the connection gets nowhere. If the first address can't be reached, one of the other family (IPv4/IPv6) is tried.
  • Redirects: with follow_redirects=True, every hop goes through the transport and is checked like the first one.
  • Checking a URL when it's given: await guard.check(url) checks it as a request would be (scheme, port, every address its host resolves to) without sending anything, so a webhook's endpoint can be refused when a user registers it. Each request is checked again all the same: DNS answers change.
  • Allowed internal destinations: allow=["billing.internal", "*.svc.cluster.local", "10.1.2.0/24"] lets those names (exact, or subdomains) and networks through although they aren't public; they're still pinned.
  • With ResilientTransport: wrap the guard in it (not the other way round): the deadline then covers the DNS lookup and each breaker is per host name. BlockedDestinationError is an httpx.RequestError but not a TransportError, so it doesn't count against the origin's breaker or trigger retry policies.
  • Connections: each host name gets an httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport of its own (sharing one SSL context), at most max_hosts (100) kept open: pinned connections are pooled by address, and two names on one address (a CDN) must not share a connection whose certificate was checked for the other. Pass a factory for your own settings, SSRFGuardTransport(lambda: httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(http2=True)), or a transport instance (a mock in tests), which then carries every request.
  • Proxies: a proxy connects on its own, so pinning can't work through it: httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(proxy=...) as the inner transport is refused. Don't pass proxy= or mounts= to the client either: those requests would bypass the transport. (The client ignores the HTTP_PROXY variables when it's given a transport.) An egress proxy that filters destinations itself, such as Smokescreen, is the alternative.

docs.title: API keys, tokens and codes

In the guide: API keys · Revoked tokens and one-time codes. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.FastAPIAPIKeys
docs.text:
FastAPIAPIKeys(lookup: Lookup[R], *, header: str = 'X-API-Key', prefix: str = 'ak', bearer: bool = False, pepper: Secrets | None = None, cache_ttl: float = 0.0, cache_size: int = 1024, scheme_name: str = 'APIKey', metrics: Metrics | None = None)

Bases: Generic[R]

FastAPI dependency that authenticates a request by its API key and returns its record.

keys = FastAPIAPIKeys(load_key, pepper=settings.api_key_pepper)

@app.get("/me")
async def me(key: Annotated[StoredKey, Depends(keys)]) -> ...

@app.delete("/orders/{id}", dependencies=[Depends(keys.require("orders:write"))])

The key comes in the header (X-API-Key by default) or, with bearer=True, as Authorization: Bearer <key>; both appear in the OpenAPI schema, for the docs' Authorize button. A missing, malformed, unknown, wrong or expired key gets the same 401 (with WWW-Authenticate); a valid key without a scope that require asks for gets a 403. Keys and secrets are never logged; put a FastAPIRateLimiter in front, since each request with a well-formed key costs a lookup.

Revoking a key: delete its record, or set its expires_at to the past. With cache_ttl, records are kept in each process for that many seconds, so a revocation takes up to that long to reach every process.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default lookup Lookup[R]

lookup(key_id): the stored record of that id, or None. Async, or a plain function, which runs in a thread like FastAPI's sync dependencies.

required header str

the request header holding the key.

'X-API-Key' prefix str

the start of every key (ak_...): letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. Secret scanners (GitHub's, GitLab's) can be taught to spot it.

'ak' bearer bool

also accept the key as Authorization: Bearer <key>.

False pepper Secrets | None

a server secret (at least 32 bytes) mixed into every digest, kept out of the database (an environment variable, a secret manager). A list rotates it: the first one is used for new keys, all of them are accepted; old peppers must stay as long as keys made with them do. Changing it without keeping the old one invalidates every key.

None cache_ttl float

seconds each process keeps a record it looked up; 0 looks up every request.

0.0 cache_size int

records kept at most per process (the least recently used are dropped).

1024 scheme_name str

name of the scheme in the OpenAPI schema.

'APIKey' metrics Metrics | None

where to count the outcomes (fastapi_alcazaba.api_keys); FastAPICache's by default.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.TokenBlocklist
docs.text:
TokenBlocklist(cache: Cache | None = None, *, namespace: str = 'revoked', fail_open: bool = False, leeway: int = 60)

Revoked tokens (by their jti) and subjects logged out everywhere (revoke_subject).

blocklist = TokenBlocklist()

async def current_user(claims: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(decode_jwt)]) -> str:
    sub, iat = claims["sub"], claims["iat"]
    if await blocklist.is_revoked(claims["jti"], subject=sub, issued_at=iat):
        raise HTTPException(401)
    return sub

Each mark lasts while the token could still be accepted, leeway included, and then the backend drops it. When the cache has a signing_key or encryption_key, the marks are sealed with it and planted ones are ignored; but whoever can delete keys in the backend can still un-revoke tokens, so keep it out of reach.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the marks; FastAPICache's by default, resolved at each call (so the blocklist can be created before FastAPICache.init).

None namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'revoked' fail_open bool

when the backend fails, is_revoked answers False (tokens are accepted) instead of True (refused, the default).

False leeway int

seconds your JWT library still accepts a token after its exp (PyJWT's leeway): marks are kept that much longer.

60

docs.title: revoke async
docs.text:
revoke(token_id: str, *, expires_at: Moment | None = None, ttl: int | None = None) -> None

Refuse the token token_id (its jti) until it would have expired anyway: give its exp as expires_at, or the seconds it has left as ttl. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails: the token isn't revoked then.

docs.title: revoke_subject async
docs.text:
revoke_subject(subject: str, *, ttl: int) -> None

Refuse every token of subject issued before the current second: log out everywhere, e.g. after a password change. ttl is the longest lifetime of your tokens. iat has whole seconds, so the tokens issued during this second stay valid, among them the one you issue right after for the current session. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails.

docs.title: is_revoked async
docs.text:
is_revoked(token_id: str, *, subject: str | None = None, issued_at: Moment | None = None) -> bool

Whether the token is refused: its jti was revoked, or its subject was logged out everywhere after it was issued (give its sub and iat). When the backend fails, not fail_open.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.OneTimeCodes
docs.text:
OneTimeCodes(secret: Secrets, cache: Cache | None = None, *, digits: int = 6, ttl: int = 300, max_attempts: int = 5, namespace: str = 'otp')

Codes of digits digits, sent by e-mail or SMS, that prove who someone is: each lasts ttl seconds, works once and is lost after max_attempts wrong guesses.

codes = OneTimeCodes(secret=settings.otp_secret)

code = await codes.issue(user.email, purpose="login")  # send it to the user
...
if not await codes.verify(form.email, form.code, purpose="login"):
    raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid or expired code")

The backend holds an HMAC of each code with secret, never the code: a plain digest of a 6-digit code is brute-forced in milliseconds by whoever reads the backend. Issuing a code replaces the previous one and gives max_attempts again, so put a FastAPIRateLimiter on the route that issues them.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default secret Secrets

at least 32 bytes (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)), from the environment or a secret manager. A list rotates them: the first one is used, all of them are accepted.

required cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the codes; FastAPICache's by default, resolved at each call.

None digits int

length of the codes, 4 to 10.

6 ttl int

seconds each code lasts.

300 max_attempts int

guesses allowed for each code, right or wrong.

5 namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'otp'

The rate limiter's sliding window: add amount to the counter key only if previous * weight + current + amount <= limit, where current is that counter and previous the counter previous_key. Returns whether it was added and both counts (current with the addition, if any).

docs.text:
InMemoryBackend(max_size: int | None = 10000)

Bases: Backend

Cache in the memory of the process: for development, tests and single-process apps.

Each instance has its own store, bounded to max_size entries (the least recently used are evicted): a store that never evicted would grow with every new query string until the process ran out of memory. State (rate-limit counters, revoked tokens, one-time codes, idempotency records: Cache.state_key) has a store of its own with the same bound, expired keys evicted first, so that caching many responses never evicts it.

docs.text:
DynamoBackend(table_name: str, region: str | None = None, *, endpoint_url: str | None = None)

Bases: Backend

Amazon DynamoDB backend provider

This backend requires an existing table within your AWS environment to be passed during backend init. If ttl is going to be used, this needs to be manually enabled on the table using the ttl key. Dynamo will take care of deleting outdated objects, but this is not instant so don't be alarmed when they linger around for a bit.

As with all AWS clients, credentials will be taken from the environment. Check the AWS SDK for more information.

Usage: >> dynamodb = DynamoBackend(table_name="your-cache", region="eu-west-1") >> await dynamodb.init() >> FastAPICache.init(dynamodb)

endpoint_url points to DynamoDB Local, LocalStack or a VPC endpoint.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.backends.tiered.TieredBackend
docs.text:
TieredBackend(remote: Backend, *, local_ttl: int = 5, local_max_size: int = 1000, invalidation_channel: str | None = 'fastapi_alcazaba:invalidations')

Bases: Backend

Two levels: a small cache in the memory of each process in front of a shared backend.

A hit in the process skips the network. Each local copy lives at most local_ttl seconds and never longer than the shared entry, which bounds how stale it can get when another process changes the value.

With a Redis or Valkey shared backend whose client supports pub/sub (RedisBackend, ValkeyBackend; not a valkey-py cluster), writes, clears and tag invalidations are announced on invalidation_channel, and every process drops its copy right away (a tag invalidation names the keys it deleted; beyond 1000, every process drops all its copies). Local copies are only kept while the process is subscribed: when the subscription drops (and messages may have been missed), the local level is emptied and bypassed until it's back. A value read from the shared backend while an invalidation arrives isn't kept: it may be the old one.

Values are kept locally as the shared backend stores them, so signed or encrypted entries stay signed or encrypted in memory too.

Scheduled jobs, the task queue, leader election and locks shared by every process. In fastapi_alcazaba.background.

In the guide: Scheduled jobs · Task queue · Leader election · Locks. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.background.FastAPIScheduler
docs.text:
FastAPIScheduler(cache: Cache | None = None, *, fail_open: bool = False, grace: float = 10.0)

Runs jobs on a schedule in each process, each tick once across them all.

Start it with the app: FastAPI(lifespan=scheduler.lifespan), or async with scheduler: inside your own lifespan (after FastAPICache.init).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cache Cache | None

where the ticks are claimed; FastAPICache's by default, resolved at start(). Not needed when every job has exclusive=False.

None fail_open bool

when the backend fails, run the exclusive jobs anyway, maybe in every process, instead of skipping the tick (the default).

False grace float

seconds stop() waits for the jobs that are running before cancelling them.

10.0

docs.title: every
docs.text:
every(*, seconds: float = 0, minutes: float = 0, hours: float = 0, days: float = 0, name: str | None = None, exclusive: bool = True) -> Callable[[F], F]

Run the decorated function (async, or sync in a thread; no arguments) every interval, at multiples of it since the Unix epoch: every(hours=1) runs on the hour (UTC). For other times, use cron.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str | None

the job's name in the backend, logs and metrics; the function's module and name by default. Two jobs can't have the same.

None exclusive bool

run each tick in one process only.

True

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.background.FastAPITaskQueue
docs.text:
FastAPITaskQueue(cache: Cache | None = None, *, name: str = 'default', concurrency: int = 10, grace: float = 10.0, poll_interval: float = 1.0, visibility_timeout: float = 60.0, max_deliveries: int = 5, max_payload_size: int = 65536, max_length: int = 100000, max_dead_letters: int = 10000)

Tasks that run in the background, in any process sharing the cache's backend.

Every process enqueues; those that call start() (or use lifespan or async with) also run tasks. A worker-only process: async with queue: await asyncio.Event().wait().

Needs Redis 6.2+ or Valkey through RedisBackend or ValkeyBackend (or a TieredBackend in front of one). Its keys are state keys (Cache.state_key), which clear() never deletes.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cache Cache | None

whose backend holds the queue; FastAPICache's by default, resolved when first needed.

None name str

queues with different names are independent.

'default' concurrency int

tasks run at a time by start() in this process.

10 grace float

seconds stop() waits for the tasks that are running; those still running then are cancelled and go back to the queue (a sync task's thread can't be stopped: it runs to its end, so that task may run twice).

10.0 poll_interval float

seconds between looks at the backend when there's nothing to do. A task enqueued in this process wakes its workers at once.

1.0 visibility_timeout float

seconds after which the tasks of a worker that stopped answering (its process died) are taken over by another. Running tasks are kept from it every third of it, however long they run.

60.0 max_deliveries int

times a task is handed to a worker (once, plus each time it's taken over from a worker that died) before it goes to the dead letters instead: it may be what kills them.

5 max_payload_size int

largest arguments, in bytes of JSON; anything larger is refused.

65536 max_length int

most tasks the queue holds (waiting, running or delayed); enqueue raises QueueFull beyond, instead of dropping tasks.

100000 max_dead_letters int

dead letters kept, about: the oldest go first.

10000

docs.title: task
docs.text:
task(name: str | None = None, *, retries: int = 3, backoff: float = 1.0, max_backoff: float = 600.0) -> Callable[[F], F]

Register the decorated function (async, or sync run in a thread) as a task. What it returns is ignored: keep results elsewhere.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str | None

the task's name in the queue, which travels with every task (keep it when the function moves); the function's module and name by default.

None retries int

times a task that raised is tried again: backoff seconds after the first failure, twice that after the second... up to max_backoff, each with jitter. Then it goes to the dead letters. 0: at the first failure.

3

docs.title: enqueue async
docs.text:
enqueue(task: Callable[..., Any] | str, /, *args: Any, delay: float | timedelta | None = None, **kwargs: Any) -> str

Queue a run of task (a registered function, or its name) with these arguments, to start in delay seconds or as soon as a worker is free; returns the task's ID.

The arguments must fit the function and be JSON-serialisable (checked here, raising TypeError); they arrive as JSON gives them back: tuples as lists, dict keys as strings. A task can't take an argument named delay by keyword. Raises QueueFull when the queue holds max_length tasks, and BackendUnavailable when the backend fails.

docs.text:
Lock(cache: Cache, name: str, *, ttl: float = 30.0, wait: float | None = 0.0, renew: bool = True, record_wait: bool = True)

A lock named name in the cache's backend (Cache.lock creates them).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ttl float

seconds after which the lock expires if its holder neither renews nor releases it.

30.0 wait float | None

seconds to wait for the lock when someone else holds it; 0 tries once, None waits as long as it takes.

0.0 renew bool

keep renewing it while it's held.

True record_wait bool

record the time spent acquiring it (fastapi_alcazaba.lock.wait); off for the locks that are tried over and over (concurrency slots, leader elections).

True

docs.text:
held: bool

Acquired, not released, and not expired since the last renewal.

docs.title: acquire async
docs.text:
acquire() -> bool

Take the lock, waiting up to wait seconds; False if someone else still holds it. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails: without it nobody can tell who holds the lock.

docs.title: release async
docs.text:
release() -> None

Release it, if this Lock holds it. A backend failure is only logged: the lock expires after ttl anyway.

docs.title: Sessions, CSRF and security headers
docs.text:
What a cookie-based app needs: server-side sessions, CSRF protection, headers and body limits. In fastapi_alcazaba.security.

In the guide: Server-side sessions · CSRF protection · Security headers and body size. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.security.ServerSessionMiddleware
docs.text:
ServerSessionMiddleware(app: ASGIApp, *, cache: Cache | None = None, cookie_name: str = 'session', max_age: int = 14 * 24 * 3600, idle_timeout: int | None = None, secure: bool = True, same_site: SameSite = 'lax', path: str = '/', domain: str | None = None, max_size: int = 16384, namespace: str = 'session')

ASGI middleware that keeps each browser's session in the cache's backend, under a random id carried by a cookie (HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite by default).

app.add_middleware(ServerSessionMiddleware)
  • Saved only when it changed, when the response starts; an empty session isn't stored and gets no cookie. A session emptied by the app is deleted and its cookie expired.
  • New ids are always the server's: a cookie whose session doesn't exist (expired, made up) never becomes the id of a new one. rotate_session at login, clear_session at logout.
  • Expiry: max_age seconds after the session was created (or rotated), and after idle_timeout seconds without requests. Both are checked when it's read, and the backend drops it then too.
  • Backend failures: if the session can't be read, the request goes on with an empty one (anonymous: fail closed) and a warning; a change to it, or any failure to save, rotate or clear, replaces the response with a 503 and leaves the cookie alone, since what the response says (logged in, logged out) wouldn't be true. Several requests of the same session at once: the last one to save wins.
  • Sealed with the cache's signing_key or encryption_key (use the latter when sessions hold personal data). Without either, whoever can write to the backend can forge sessions: a warning is logged.
  • WebSockets get websocket.session too, read-only.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cache Cache | None

where sessions are kept; the app's (Cache.install) or FastAPICache's by default. With a TieredBackend, only its shared (remote) tier is used.

None cookie_name str

the cookie. __Host-session keeps sibling subdomains from setting one (cookie tossing); it needs secure, path / and no domain.

'session' max_age int

seconds a session lasts from its creation; also the cookie's Max-Age.

14 * 24 * 3600 idle_timeout int | None

seconds without requests after which it's over; None for no limit.

None secure bool

only send the cookie over HTTPS.

True same_site SameSite

the cookie's SameSite: "lax", "strict" or "none" (needs secure).

'lax' path str

the cookie's path.

'/' domain str | None

the cookie's domain; None keeps it to the host that set it.

None max_size int

bytes of JSON a session may take; more raises ValueError when it's saved.

16384 namespace str

part of the backend keys, after the cache's prefix (Cache.state_key).

'session'

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.security.rotate_session
docs.text:
rotate_session(connection: HTTPConnection) -> None

Give the session a new id, with the same data, when the response starts. Call it when the user logs in or gains privileges: an id someone planted in their browser before (session fixation) is deleted with the old session. The new session's max_age starts then.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.security.clear_session
docs.text:
clear_session(connection: HTTPConnection) -> None

Log out: empty the session, delete it from the backend and expire the cookie when the response starts. Data stored afterwards in the same request goes to a new session.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.security.ServerSession
docs.text:
ServerSession(data: dict[str, Any] | None = None)

Bases: dict[str, Any]

The session of a request (request.session): a dict of JSON values, saved when the response starts if it changed (nested changes too).

Once it's read the response depends on the cookie, and gets Vary: Cookie. Starlette 1.0+ tells it on every request.session; older ones don't, so its reads tell it too.

docs.title: mark_accessed
docs.text:
mark_accessed() -> None

Called by request.session: the response then depends on the cookie.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.security.CSRFMiddleware
docs.text:
CSRFMiddleware(app: ASGIApp, *, trusted_origins: Iterable[str] = (), exempt_paths: Iterable[str] = (), require_token: bool = False, check_all: bool = False, cookie_name: str = '__Host-csrftoken', header_name: str = 'X-CSRF-Token', cookie_secure: bool = True, cookie_domain: str | None = None)

ASGI middleware that refuses, with a 403, unsafe requests that a page on another site made the user's browser send. See the module's documentation for the rules.

app.add_middleware(CSRFMiddleware)

The app's own origin is the scheme and the Host header as the server sees them. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, let the server trust it (uvicorn --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=<proxy address>) so that the scheme is https, and have the proxy pass the Host header on; otherwise list the public origin in trusted_origins.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default trusted_origins Iterable[str]

other origins (https://admin.example.com) whose pages may send requests: sibling subdomains count as other origins, and so do identity providers and payment pages that post a form back to the app.

() exempt_paths Iterable[str]

path prefixes that aren't checked (webhooks signed in their own way). They're matched like the app's routes: without the root_path a proxy or a mount adds.

() require_token bool

also require, on requests with cookies, a header (header_name) equal to the token cookie (cookie_name) set on every response that lacks a valid one. The token is in request.state.csrf_token too. A request whose browser sends neither Origin nor Referer passes with a valid token.

False check_all bool

also check requests without cookies or HTTP authentication: for apps that trust TLS client certificates or the network (an intranet), which the browser sends too.

False cookie_name str

the token cookie. The __Host- prefix keeps sibling subdomains from setting one (cookie tossing); it needs cookie_secure and no cookie_domain.

'__Host-csrftoken' header_name str

the header that carries the token.

'X-CSRF-Token' cookie_secure bool

only send the token cookie over HTTPS.

True cookie_domain str | None

the token cookie's domain, for pages on another subdomain that need to read it (then pick a name without the __Host- prefix).

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.security.SecurityHeadersMiddleware
docs.text:
SecurityHeadersMiddleware(app: ASGIApp, *, headers: Mapping[str, str | None] | None = None, hsts: str | None = 'max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains', csp: str | None = "default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'", html_csp: str | None = None)

Adds the security headers of the OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet to every response, without overwriting the ones the app sets itself.

app.add_middleware(SecurityHeadersMiddleware)
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin on every response.
  • Strict-Transport-Security only on HTTPS requests: on plain HTTP browsers ignore it, and on a development localhost it would stick. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, tell the server to trust it (uvicorn --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=<proxy address>) so that the request's scheme is https.
  • Content-Security-Policy: csp for responses that aren't HTML (nothing in a JSON response should load anything), html_csp for HTML ones. None by default, so that FastAPI's Swagger UI and ReDoc, which load scripts from a CDN, keep working.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default headers Mapping[str, str | None] | None

more headers, or other values for the defaults; None removes a default.

None hsts str | None

the Strict-Transport-Security value; None leaves it out.

'max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains' csp str | None

the Content-Security-Policy of responses that aren't HTML; None leaves it out.

"default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'" html_csp str | None

the Content-Security-Policy of HTML responses.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.security.BodySizeLimitMiddleware
docs.text:
BodySizeLimitMiddleware(app: ASGIApp, *, max_size: int = 1048576, paths: Mapping[str, int | None] | None = None)

Refuses request bodies larger than max_size bytes with a 413. FastAPI has no limit of its own: a client could send an endless body that the app reads into memory.

app.add_middleware(BodySizeLimitMiddleware, max_size=1_048_576, paths={"/uploads": None})

A Content-Length over the limit is refused before the app runs. Bodies without one (chunked) are counted while the app reads them, and refused as soon as they pass the limit.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default max_size int

the limit, in bytes.

1048576 paths Mapping[str, int | None] | None

other limits for the paths starting with these prefixes (the longest matching prefix wins; None for no limit). They're matched like the app's routes: without the root_path a proxy or a mount adds in front.

None

docs.title: limit
docs.text:
limit(path: str) -> int | None

The limit for requests to path; None when there's none.

docs.title: Response cache
docs.text:
Cache, FastAPICache, the @cache decorator, key builders and coders. In fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache.

In the guide: Quick start · Configuration · Coders · Key builders. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache.Cache
docs.text:
Cache(backend: Backend, prefix: str = '', expire: int | None = None, coder: type[Coder] = JsonCoder, key_builder: KeyBuilder = default_key_builder, cache_status: str | None = 'Alcazaba', enable: bool = True, *, signing_key: Secrets | None = None, encryption_key: Secrets | None = None, vary_headers: Iterable[str] = DEFAULT_VARY_HEADERS, respect_cache_control: bool = False, single_flight: bool = True, backend_timeout: float | None = 1.0, circuit_breaker_failures: int | None = 5, circuit_breaker_reset: float = 30.0, max_value_size: int | None = None, distributed_lock: bool = False, lock_timeout: float = 10.0, lock_wait: float = 5.0, early_refresh: float | None = None, compression: Codec | None = None, compression_min_size: int = 1024, compression_level: int | None = None, metrics: bool = True, meter_provider: Any = None, tracing: bool = True, tracer_provider: Any = None)

A cache: a backend and its settings. Create one per app, or several (e.g. a public one and an encrypted one for personal data), and decorate with cached(); or use the global FastAPICache with @cache.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default backend Backend

where entries are stored.

required prefix str

prefix of every key.

'' expire int | None

default time to live, in seconds.

None coder type[Coder]

how values are stored (JsonCoder by default).

JsonCoder key_builder KeyBuilder

builds keys from the function and its arguments.

default_key_builder cache_status str | None

this cache's name in the responses' Cache-Status header (RFC 9211): Alcazaba; hit; ttl=42 for a hit, else why the request reached the endpoint (fwd=miss, stale, request, method, bypass) and whether the result was stored. A token (letters, digits and !#$%&'*+-.^_|~:/`, starting with a letter); None for no header.

'Alcazaba' enable bool

False turns the cache off.

True signing_key Secrets | None

secret (at least 32 bytes; text, bytes, or pydantic's SecretStr or SecretBytes) used to sign every entry with HMAC-SHA256; entries without a valid signature are ignored. Strongly recommended when the backend is shared or reachable by others, and needed for PickleCoder. A list of keys rotates them: the first one signs, all of them are accepted.

None encryption_key Secrets | None

like signing_key, but the entries are also encrypted (AES-256-GCM): a dump or a backup of the backend doesn't reveal the cached responses. Needs the crypto extra. Use one or the other, not both.

None vary_headers Iterable[str]

request headers that give each value its own cache entry and make the response private (see DEFAULT_VARY_HEADERS). Pass () for endpoints whose response is the same for everybody.

DEFAULT_VARY_HEADERS respect_cache_control bool

let clients skip the cache with Cache-Control: no-cache or no-store. Off by default: anyone could otherwise make every request reach the endpoint, which defeats the cache as a shield against load.

False single_flight bool

concurrent misses for the same key wait for the first one instead of all computing the value (cache stampede protection), within each process.

True backend_timeout float | None

seconds each backend call may take before the cache is skipped for that request; None waits as long as the client does.

1.0 circuit_breaker_failures int | None

consecutive backend failures after which the backend is not called for circuit_breaker_reset seconds (requests run uncached and don't wait for it); None disables the breaker.

5 max_value_size int | None

values larger than this many bytes (once encoded) aren't stored.

None distributed_lock bool

on a miss, take a lock in the backend so that a single process computes the value while the others wait for it (up to lock_wait seconds, then they compute it themselves). The lock expires after lock_timeout seconds.

False early_refresh float | None

fraction of the lifetime at its end in which a hit may recompute the value (more likely as the expiry nears), so that popular entries are refreshed before they expire instead of all callers missing at once. E.g. 0.1.

None compression Codec | None

"zstd" (Python 3.14, or the zstd extra) or "zlib": entries of at least compression_min_size bytes are stored compressed when that makes them smaller, with compression_level (the codec's default if None). Compressed entries are read back whatever this setting, so it can be turned on and off freely.

None metrics bool

record OpenTelemetry metrics (needs the otel extra).

True meter_provider Any

OpenTelemetry meter provider; the global one by default.

None tracing bool

record OpenTelemetry spans of cached calls and backend calls (otel extra).

True tracer_provider Any

OpenTelemetry tracer provider; the global one by default.

None

docs.title: get_or_set async
docs.text:
get_or_set(key: str, compute: Callable[[], Awaitable[T]], *, expire: int | None = None, namespace: str = '', tags: Tags | None = None) -> T

The value cached under key, or else await compute(), stored. For caching inside an endpoint what doesn't fit a decorator. Same pipeline as cached() (signing, encryption, compression, single flight, locks); annotate compute's return type to get it back as that type. The key is hashed: user input in it never reaches the backend in clear.

docs.title: state_key
docs.text:
state_key(kind: str, rest: str) -> str

Backend key of state other than cached responses: locks, rate-limit counters, revoked tokens, one-time codes, idempotency records. It goes under {prefix}!, not {prefix}:, so that clear() never frees a held lock, resets a rate limit or takes a revocation back, and InMemoryBackend keeps it apart from the entries it evicts.

docs.text:
tag_key(tag: str) -> str

Backend key of a tag. The digest goes in {braces} (a cluster hash tag) so that the set and its temporary copy share a slot, whatever characters the tag has.

get_cache(request: HTTPConnection) -> Cache

FastAPI dependency: the cache installed on the app (Cache.install), else FastAPICache's. Works in WebSocket routes too.

@app.post("/products/{product_id}")

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache.FastAPICache
docs.text: The global cache that @cache uses: a Cache configured once with init(). For several caches, or one per app, create Cache instances instead.

docs.title: init classmethod

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.core.Signer
docs.text:
Signer(keys: Secrets)

Signs what the cache stores and only accepts what it signed itself.

Whoever can write to the backend (a shared Redis, a leaked password) can't plant data, nor a pickle that runs code when it's read, nor copy one user's entry under another user's key: the tag covers the key too. The first key signs; the others are only checked, so a key can be rotated without losing the cache: put the new one first and drop the old one later.

docs.text:
unsign(cache_key: str, data: bytes) -> bytes | None

The payload, or None when data wasn't signed by us for this key.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.core.canonical_json
docs.text:
canonical_json(value: Any) -> bytes

value (dicts with string keys, lists, tuples, strings, integers, floats, booleans and None) in its canonical form, as UTF-8. Raises ValueError for what I-JSON leaves out (integers a double can't hold exactly, NaN, infinities, lone surrogates) and TypeError for what isn't JSON.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.core.Encrypter
docs.text:
Encrypter(keys: Secrets)

Encrypts what the cache stores and only accepts what it encrypted itself.

On top of what signing gives (whoever can write to the backend can't plant data, run a pickle or move one user's entry under another user's key), a dump or a backup of Redis doesn't reveal the cached responses. The cache key is the associated data, so an entry only decrypts under its own key. Each entry is encrypted with its own AES-256 key, derived with HKDF-SHA256 from the secret and a random salt, so random 96-bit nonces never get near the limits of AES-GCM however many entries are written.

The first secret encrypts; all of them decrypt, so a secret can be rotated without losing the cache: put the new one first and drop the old one later.

Layout: b"fastapi_alcazaba/e1" | key id (4) | salt (16) | nonce (12) | ciphertext and GCM tag (16).

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.core.CircuitBreaker
docs.text:
CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold: int = 5, reset_timeout: float = 30.0)

Stops calling a failing backend for a while.

Closed: calls go through, and failure_threshold consecutive failures open it. Open: calls are refused for reset_timeout seconds. Then a single trial call goes through (half open): a success closes it, a failure opens it again. One breaker per process.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit.FastAPIRateLimiter
docs.text:
FastAPIRateLimiter(times: int = 1, milliseconds: int = 0, seconds: int = 0, minutes: int = 0, hours: int = 0, identifier: Identifier | None = None, callback: OnLimit | None = None, *, name: str | None = None, cache: Cache | None = None, fail_open: bool = True, cost: int = 1, headers: bool = True)

FastAPI dependency that lets each client make times requests per window to a route; the next ones get a 429 with Retry-After until the window slides past enough of them.

@app.get("/search", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(times=10, minutes=1))])

The counters live in the cache's backend (the cache given, else the one get_cache returns), so every process shares them, and go through its timeout and circuit breaker. Their keys are SHA-256 digests: identities never reach the backend in clear.

It's a sliding window: the count of the previous window is added in proportion to how much of it is still less than a window ago, so no client doubles its rate around the boundary between two windows. That assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly; when they came at its end, it's a little stricter than times per window. Requests over the limit don't count: checking and counting is one atomic operation where the backend allows it. Each process then refuses a client with nothing left without asking the backend, until something fits again, so a flood doesn't reach the backend.

Responses carry the RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers of the IETF draft (draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers), for clients to slow down before they get a 429.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default times int

requests allowed per window.

1 milliseconds int

the window is the sum of milliseconds, seconds, minutes and hours.

0 identifier Identifier | None

who the client is; its address by default (client_ip). E.g. a user id.

None callback OnLimit | None

called with the request and the seconds to wait when a request is over the limit; too_many_requests by default. If it returns, the request goes on.

None name str | None

the routes using limiters with this name and the same rate share one budget; by default each route (its methods and path template) has its own. Also the policy's name in the headers.

None cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the counters.

None fail_open bool

when the backend fails, let requests through (the default, as the cache does) or refuse them with a 503.

True cost int

how much of the budget each request takes: an expensive route can take more of a budget it shares with others (name).

1 headers bool

send the RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers.

True

docs.text:
FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter(limit: int, *, name: str | None = None, identifier: Identifier | None = None, wait: float = 0.0, ttl: float = 60.0, cache: Cache | None = None, fail_open: bool = True, retry_after: int = 1)

@app.post("/summaries", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter(8, wait=5))])

docs.title: slot async
docs.text:
slot(key: str = '', *, connection: HTTPConnection | None = None) -> AsyncIterator[None]

Hold a slot around a block, outside a dependency:

async with limiter.slot(key=tenant_id):
    await render(report)

key gives each value its own limit slots. With a connection, the route and the identifier apply as in the dependency; without one, the limiter needs a name. Raises ConcurrencyLimitExceeded when no slot frees within wait seconds, and BackendUnavailable when the backend fails and fail_open is False.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.observability.FastAPIProblemDetails
docs.text:
FastAPIProblemDetails(*, expose_detail: bool = True, max_errors: int = 100)

Answers errors with RFC 9457 problem details. install(app) handles:

  • HTTPException (FastAPI's and Starlette's, and subclasses such as BreakerOpen and Problem), keeping its headers (Retry-After, WWW-Authenticate...). A 4xx's detail is sent, since it's written for clients (expose_detail=False keeps it); a 5xx's never is, except a Problem's. Codes under 400 (redirects raised as exceptions) keep FastAPI's answer.
  • RequestValidationError: a 422 whose errors list each error's loc, msg and type, never its input (which echoes what was sent, passwords included) nor its ctx.

  • any other exception: a 500 that says nothing about it. Starlette raises the exception again after the response, so that the server logs it with its traceback (uvicorn's "Exception in ASGI application") and TestClient raises it in tests (raise_server_exceptions=False to see the response). With debug=True, Starlette answers with its traceback page instead.

    FastAPIProblemDetails().install(app)

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default expose_detail bool

send the detail of 4xx HTTPExceptions.

True max_errors int

validation errors listed at most, so that a huge invalid body doesn't get a huge answer.

Register the handlers in app, before it starts. A handler you register for a status code or an exception subclass still wins for those. Alcazaba's middlewares answer with problems too (the 504 of a timeout, the 413 of a body too large...).

Add it last, the outermost, so that every log line and every answer of the other middlewares carry the ID. When the app raises, the ID stays set for the rest of the request's task: the error handler and the server log the exception outside every middleware.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.observability.request_id
docs.text:
A request ID for every request, to find all the log lines of one request and to let a client quote it when it reports an error.

app.add_middleware(RequestIDMiddleware)  # last: the outermost

handler.addFilter(RequestIDLogFilter())  # then "%(request_id)s" in the format

RequestIDMiddleware takes the ID from the request's X-Request-ID (set by a proxy or the client) when it's safe to log, else makes a random one; request_id() returns it anywhere while the request is handled, and the response carries it in the same header. An incoming ID is reused only if it matches [A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,128}: anything else (line breaks that would forge log lines, an endless value) gets a new one.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.observability.RequestTimeoutMiddleware
docs.text:
RequestTimeoutMiddleware(app: ASGIApp, *, timeout: float | None = 30.0, paths: Mapping[str, float | None] | None = None)

Gives every HTTP request timeout seconds, from its arrival until its response has been sent; WebSockets and lifespan events go through untouched.

app.add_middleware(RequestTimeoutMiddleware, timeout=30, paths={"/exports": None})
  • Out of time before the response starts: the app is cancelled and the client gets a 504 with a small JSON body.
  • Out of time while a response streams: too late for a 504. The app is cancelled and the exception (a TimeoutError) raised again, so that the server closes the connection: the client sees an incomplete body, never a short one that looks complete. Give streaming endpoints (Server-Sent Events, big exports) their own limit in paths, or None.
  • Once the response has been sent, background tasks have no deadline.
  • Sync endpoints run in a thread that can't be interrupted: the client gets its 504 on time, but the thread runs to its end, after the exit of its yield dependencies has run. Endpoints that may hit the deadline are better async.

Both cases are logged as warnings.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default timeout float | None

the deadline, in seconds; None for none.

30.0 paths Mapping[str, float | None] | None

other deadlines for the paths starting with these prefixes (the longest matching prefix wins; None for none), matched like the app's routes: without the root_path a proxy or a mount adds in front.

None

docs.text:
FastAPIPaginationCursor(secret: Secrets | None = None, *, default_size: int = 50, max_size: int = 100)

Pagination by cursor: ?size=20, then ?size=20&cursor=<next_cursor>.

cursors = FastAPIPaginationCursor(secret=settings.cursor_secret)

@app.get("/events")
@cache(expire=60)
async def events(params: Annotated[CursorParams, Depends(cursors)]) -> CursorPage[Event]:
    rows = ...  # WHERE (created_at, id) > params.after ... LIMIT params.limit
    return cursors.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda e: (e.created_at, e.id), queried=True)

A cursor is the sort key of a page's last item, base64-encoded: clients can read it, so sort by what they may see. With a secret it's signed too (HMAC-SHA256), and a cursor that a client made or changed gets a 400 like any other invalid one, before the endpoint runs; without it, the values are only checked to be of the types a sort key can have.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default secret Secrets | None

at least 32 bytes (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)); a list rotates them, the first one signing and all of them accepted. None for unsigned cursors.

None default_size int

items per page when the request doesn't say.

50 max_size int

the most a request may ask for (a 422 beyond).

100

docs.title: Checking uploads
docs.text:
The type of a file from its bytes, its size and pixels, and safe file names. In fastapi_alcazaba.uploads.

In the guide: Checking uploads. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.uploads.FastAPIUploads
docs.text:
FastAPIUploads(types: str | Collection[str], *, max_size: int = 10 * 1024 * 1024, max_pixels: int | None = 40000000, metrics: Metrics | None = None)

Checks uploaded files: their type from their bytes, their size and, for images, their dimensions. Use it as a dependency for a form field named file, or call check():

uploads = FastAPIUploads(types={"application/pdf"}, max_size=20 * 1024 * 1024)

@app.post("/invoices")
async def invoice(upload: Annotated[CheckedFile, Depends(uploads)]) -> Invoice: ...

@app.post("/albums")
async def album(photos: list[UploadFile]) -> Album:
    checked = [await photo_uploads.check(photo) for photo in photos]

The upload is read in chunks and counted, whatever UploadFile.size says. By the time an endpoint runs, the multipart parser has already stored the whole request, so keep its size down with BodySizeLimitMiddleware on the route as well.

It doesn't look inside the files: a PDF can carry scripts, an Office document macros (the macro-enabled types are told apart from the others), ZIP and GZIP archives may expand to far more than their size, and the frames of a GIF aren't counted. HTML, SVG and XML run scripts in a browser: allow them only to serve them from another domain, as attachments.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default types str | Collection[str]

the types accepted, from KNOWN_TYPES (IMAGES, OFFICE_DOCUMENTS...).

required max_size int

the largest file accepted, in bytes; larger ones get a 413.

10 * 1024 * 1024 max_pixels int | None

the most pixels (width × height) an image may have; more gets a 413. None for no limit. Images whose dimensions can't be read get a 415 either way.

40000000 metrics Metrics | None

where to count the outcomes (fastapi_alcazaba.uploads); FastAPICache's by default.

None

docs.text:

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.uploads.sniff
docs.text:
sniff(data: bytes) -> str | None

The type of a file from its bytes, whatever its name or the type the client said; None when it isn't one of KNOWN_TYPES.

The first bytes are enough (a few dozen; 4096 to tell HTML and SVG from other XML), except to tell Office documents from other ZIP archives, which takes the whole file. Text must be UTF-8 (or ASCII) without control characters throughout data, which may end in a cut character. CSV is text: it can't be told apart from other text.

(width, height) of a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP image, read from its headers without decoding it; None for other files and when they can't be read. A JPEG may need more than its first bytes: its frame header comes after its metadata.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.uploads.safe_filename
docs.text:
safe_filename(name: str | None, *, default: str = 'file', max_length: int = 255) -> str

A version of a client's file name that's safe to show, and to use on any file system: NFKC-normalised, only what follows the last / or \, without control or invisible characters (such as the right-to-left override that disguises exe.txt as txt.exe), with <>:"|?* replaced by _, without leading dots, spaces or dashes (hidden files, command-line options) nor trailing dots and spaces (which Windows drops), _ before the names Windows reserves (CON, NUL, COM1...), and shortened to max_length bytes of UTF-8, keeping the extension. default when nothing is left.

It doesn't make the extension match the content: store files under a name of your own with CheckedFile.extension, and keep this one for display or Content-Disposition.

docs.title: Webhooks and outbound calls
docs.text:
Standard Webhooks in and out, and httpx transports with deadlines, breakers and SSRF checks. In fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks and fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.

In the guide: Signed webhooks · Outbound calls. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks.FastAPIWebhooks
docs.text:
FastAPIWebhooks(secret: WebhookSecrets, *, tolerance: int = 300, cache: Cache | None = None, max_body_size: int = 1048576, namespace: str = 'webhook', fail_open: bool = False)

FastAPI dependency that accepts only webhooks signed with secret, and each delivery once.

webhooks = FastAPIWebhooks(settings.webhook_secret)

@app.post("/webhooks")
async def receive(message: Annotated[WebhookMessage, Depends(webhooks)]) -> None: ...

It reads the raw body (up to max_body_size bytes, a 413 beyond) and leaves it in the request, for message.json() or await request.json(). Validate it there, not with a pydantic body parameter: FastAPI reads and validates those before any dependency, without the size limit and before the signature is checked. It can't read a body the endpoint takes as a form, which consumes it first: webhooks are JSON.

Missing or malformed headers get a 400; a wrong signature, a timestamp more than tolerance seconds away from the server's clock (either way) and a delivery accepted before all get the same 401, which doesn't say which check failed.

Replays: each delivery accepted (its id and timestamp, hashed) is counted in the cache's backend until its timestamp can't be accepted anymore, so every process refuses it again. A retry of the sender has a new timestamp and signature and goes through: Standard Webhooks keeps the id of a message for all its attempts, and a retry after a failed (5xx) attempt must get through. So make the endpoint idempotent on message.id (a unique constraint), as the specification advises, if a message must not be processed twice. Whoever can write to the backend can delete the marks (and allow a replay within tolerance): keep it out of reach.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default secret WebhookSecrets

whsec_<base64>, the base64 alone or raw bytes, at least 24 bytes once decoded. A list rotates them: a signature by any of them is accepted.

required tolerance int

seconds a timestamp may be away from the server's clock, either way.

300 cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend counts the deliveries (it must support counters); the app's (Cache.install) or FastAPICache's by default.

None max_body_size int

larger bodies get a 413 without being read to the end.

1048576 namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'webhook' fail_open bool

when the backend fails, accept the (correctly signed) webhook without the replay check instead of answering 503. Off by default: senders retry a 503 later, while a replay would run its effects again.

False

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.ResilientTransport
docs.text:
ResilientTransport(transport: AsyncBaseTransport | None = None, *, timeout: float | None = 10.0, failure_threshold: int | None = 5, reset_timeout: float = 30.0, failure_statuses: Collection[int] = (500, 502, 503, 504), max_response_size: int | None = None, metrics: Metrics | None = None)

Bases: AsyncBaseTransport

An httpx transport that gives every call a deadline and every origin a circuit breaker.

client = httpx.AsyncClient(transport=ResilientTransport(timeout=5), base_url=...)

Responses are read whole within the deadline before they're returned, so don't stream large downloads through it; max_response_size bounds what it reads.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default transport AsyncBaseTransport | None

the transport that sends the requests; httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport() by default (pass your own for its verify, limits, proxy...).

None timeout float | None

seconds for the whole call, from sending the request to the last byte of the response; httpx.TimeoutException beyond. It applies to each request the transport sends: with follow_redirects, every hop gets a deadline of its own. None for no deadline (httpx's own timeouts still apply).

10.0 failure_threshold int | None

consecutive failures of an origin (scheme, host and port) after which it isn't called for reset_timeout seconds; then a single trial call decides whether it's back. Transport errors and timeouts count; errors of the caller's own (an illegal header value, an unsupported URL scheme, a request body that raises) don't. None disables the breaker.

5 reset_timeout float

seconds an open breaker refuses calls.

30.0 failure_statuses Collection[int]

response statuses that count as failures, besides errors and timeouts. The response is still returned.

(500, 502, 503, 504) max_response_size int | None

bytes of response body read at most, as they come (before Content-Encoding is decoded); ResponseTooLargeError beyond, which isn't a failure of the origin. None for no limit.

None metrics Metrics | None

where to count breakers opening and refusing calls (fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.breaker); FastAPICache's by default.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.SSRFGuardTransport
docs.text:
SSRFGuardTransport(transport: InnerTransport | None = None, *, allow: Iterable[AllowedDestination] = (), ports: Collection[int] | None = None, max_hosts: int = 100, metrics: Metrics | None = None)

Bases: AsyncBaseTransport

An httpx transport that only calls the public internet: no private, loopback, link-local (cloud metadata), multicast or reserved addresses, whatever the URL says.

client = httpx.AsyncClient(transport=ResilientTransport(SSRFGuardTransport()))

It resolves the host itself and refuses the request (BlockedDestinationError) if any of its addresses isn't public, IPv6 forms of IPv4 addresses (::ffff:127.0.0.1, NAT64, 6to4) and numeric spellings (2130706433, 0x7f.1) included. Then it connects to the address it checked: the URL is rewritten to it, the Host header keeps the name, and TLS gets the name for SNI and the certificate check. A DNS server that answers a public address to the check and a private one to the connection (DNS rebinding) gets nowhere. Each hop of a redirect comes through the transport again and is checked like the first.

Wrap it in ResilientTransport rather than the other way round: the deadline then covers the DNS lookup, and each breaker is per host name. Give the transport to the client, not as one of its mounts, and give the client no proxy: those requests wouldn't go through it. A proxy in the inner transport is refused: it would connect on its own (an egress proxy that filters destinations, such as Smokescreen, is the alternative to this transport, not its companion).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default transport InnerTransport | None

what sends the requests. By default each host name gets an httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport of its own, sharing one SSL context: connections are pooled by address, and two names on the same address (a CDN, a shared host) must not share one, whose certificate was checked for the other name. Pass a function returning a transport (e.g. lambda: httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(http2=True)) to make them yourself, or a transport (a mock in tests), to send everything through it.

None allow Iterable[AllowedDestination]

host names (exact, or *.example.com for its subdomains), networks and addresses that may be reached although they aren't public, e.g. an internal service: allow=["billing.internal", "10.1.2.0/24"]. Requests to them are still pinned to the address checked.

() ports Collection[int] | None

the only ports allowed (ports=(443,)); None for any.

None max_hosts int

host names with a transport of their own kept open at most (the least recently used ones without an open response are closed).

100 metrics Metrics | None

where to count refused requests (fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.ssrf.blocked); FastAPICache's by default.

None

docs.title: check async
docs.text:
check(url: URL | str, *, timeout: float | None = 5.0) -> None

Check url as a request to it would be, without sending anything: its scheme, its port and every address its host resolves to (within timeout seconds). Raises BlockedDestinationError when a request would be refused, and httpx.ConnectError when the host doesn't resolve. For a URL that users give (a webhook's endpoint), when they give it; every request is checked again all the same, as DNS answers change.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.BlockedDestinationError
docs.text:
Bases: RequestError

SSRFGuardTransport didn't send the request: its scheme, port or address isn't allowed. A limit of the client, like ResponseTooLargeError: it isn't counted against the origin.
